Roberto, you have two minutes. Start with what you want us to decide.
I want a yes to entering the premium segment next year. Here is my claim: it is the only part of this category that is growing, and it will not stay open.
That is a strong claim. What backs it up?
Four years of data on one page. Volume flat, money up nineteen percent, and every point of that came from the premium end. That is the evidence, and anybody here can check it.
My objection is simple. We are late. Our competitor has been there for two years.
We are late, and that is exactly my argument, not an answer to it. If we wait another year, we will pay three times more to enter. I have seen that happen in this company before.
And if the shelf life test fails?
If the test fails, we will not launch in March, and I will come back to this room with a new date and no excuses. What I am asking for today is the decision, not the calendar.
Then give me your takeaway in one sentence, and we will vote.
Let me start with what I want you to decide.
Every claim on this page is backed up by one number.
That is a fair point, and it is my argument, not an answer to it.
If there is one takeaway tonight, it is this number.

I prepare people for rooms where somebody can say no, and I always start in the same place. Your first sentence does about half the work, and almost everybody wastes it. Most people use it to thank the room and explain the agenda. Do not do that. Use it to say what you want them to decide. Then three parts, in this order, and only three. One: the claim. One sentence, no more. Two: the evidence that backs it up, and by evidence I mean something a person in that room can check without asking you. Three, and this is the part that wins arguments: the consequence of not deciding. Not the benefits of deciding. The cost of waiting. And one last thing, about the objection you are most afraid of. Say it yourself, out loud, before anybody else does. An objection you name loses most of its power. An objection that catches you keeps all of it, and it takes the room with it.

I had two meetings that year that I still think about, and I lost one of them for a reason that had nothing to do with the numbers. The one I won, I opened with the decision. First sentence: I want a yes on this, today, and here is why. And then I said the objection myself, before anybody could raise it. We are late, this is expensive, and here is what happens if we wait. Twenty minutes, done. The one I lost, I had better data. Genuinely better. But the first person who pushed back caught me, and instead of answering I argued with him. My tone went defensive in about four seconds, and after that nobody in that room heard a single piece of my evidence, because they were all watching two people fight. So the sentence I use now, every time, is this one: that is a fair point, and here is what happens if we do nothing about it. It costs me nothing and it keeps the room.
